item.title: 42pc of people struggle to meet healthcare costs
item.description:
Nearly 42 per cent of the country’s population faces financial hardship when paying for medical treatment. In 2022 alone, healthcare expenses pushed 7.2 million people below the poverty line. 

These findings emerged from a study by the Health Economics Unit of the Ministry of Health. The study found that the burden of medical expenses falls most heavily on the poor, with a large share of out-of-pocket spending going towards medicines.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Swedish Embassy supported the Health Economics Unit in conducting the study. Its findings were presented at a hotel in the capital on Wednesday. The study used data from the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics’ (BBS) Household Income and Expenditure Surveys conducted in 2005, 2010, 2016 and 2022.

The aim was to examine how much people spend out of their own pockets when seeking healthcare, which aspects of treatment account for their spending, and how heavily these expenses affect them.

State Minister for Health MA Muhith, the chief guest at the event, said the findings offered a striking illustration of the dire state of the health sector. The BNP was in power at the beginning of the 17-year period from 2005 to 2022, while a “fascist government” was in power for the remaining years. Therefore, he argued, the BNP government could not be held responsible for the picture that emerged from the study.

The problem is getting worse

At the beginning of the presentation, Subrata Pal, focal point for the Bangladesh National Health Accounts at the Health Economics Unit, said the country faced a contradiction in terms of financial protection.

In 2005, 40 per cent of the population was poor. By 2022, that figure had fallen to 18.7 per cent. Yet the proportion of people experiencing financial hardship or pressure rose from 12.5 per cent in 2005 to 32.1 per cent in 2022. In other words, the share of people living in poverty has declined, while the number facing financial pressure has increased.

The study found that financial hardship caused by healthcare expenses continues to grow. In 2005, 28.2 per cent of the population faced financial hardship due to medical costs. The situation has since worsened: by 2022, 41.7 per cent of people were under financial pressure while trying to pay for healthcare.

This burden affects all sections of society, including the rich, the middle class and the poor. Such financial pressure can push people below the poverty line. In 2022, healthcare expenses alone drove 7.2 million people below the poverty line, largely because a substantial portion of medical costs had to be paid out of their own pockets.

Where the Money Goes

The study did not present figures showing the amount or proportion of total healthcare expenditure paid directly by individuals. Calculating out-of-pocket expenditure (OOP) was not the study’s objective. However, it did estimate how many people pay for treatment out of their own pockets and how that money is spent.

In 2005, 52.5 per cent of people paid for medical treatment out of their own pockets. The proportion increased steadily, reaching 92.7 per cent in 2022. In 2005, the average out-of-pocket medical expenditure per household was Tk 709. By 2022, it had risen to Tk 3,493. Those who do not pay out of pocket are assumed to receive free treatment at government hospitals or NGO-run health centres.

Medicines and diagnostic tests account for the largest shares of medical expenses. In 2022, patients visiting hospital outpatient departments spent 74 per cent of their total treatment costs on medicines, while medicines accounted for 35 per cent of the expenses incurred by admitted patients. Diagnostic tests accounted for 11 per cent of out-of-pocket spending by outpatients and 22 per cent by admitted patients. Other expenses included doctors’ consultations, hospital stays and transportation.

The study also found that private hospitals are more expensive than public facilities. In 2022, the average out-of-pocket expenditure for a patient receiving treatment at a government hospital was Tk 2,688, compared with Tk 4,808 at a private hospital.

For patients admitted to hospital, the average cost was Tk 21,547 at a government hospital and Tk 32,517 at a private hospital. The average cost for admission to an NGO-run hospital was Tk 22,028.

Why Financial Hardship Is Increasing

Researchers identified several factors behind the rise in out-of-pocket spending and financial hardship.

Healthcare costs are rising faster than household incomes. The study found that household income increased by 38 per cent between 2016 and 2022, while healthcare expenditure rose by 43 per cent over the same period.

The proportion of patients requiring hospital admission has also increased. In 2016, 8.1 per cent of patients seeking treatment were admitted to hospital. By 2022, the figure had risen to 12.4 per cent. Hospital admission generally means higher out-of-pocket expenses for patients.

Another factor is the declining proportion of patients seeking treatment at government hospitals. In 2016, 15.1 per cent of patients chose government hospitals for treatment. By 2022, that share had fallen to 10.9 per cent.

At the same time, people have become increasingly reliant on pharmacies. In 2016, 32.5 per cent of people turned to pharmacies for treatment. By 2022, the proportion had risen to 55.4 per cent.

The growing prevalence of chronic diseases is another reason for the increase in financial hardship. In 2005, 44.7 per cent of patients suffered from chronic diseases. By 2022, the figure had risen to 72.4 per cent. People with chronic conditions need to take medication over long periods, and some must pay for medicines for the rest of their lives.

The Burden Is Not the Same Everywhere

People in different parts of the country do not experience the financial burden of healthcare equally. The regional pattern has also changed over time.

In 2005, the proportion of people facing financial hardship due to medical expenses was highest in Rajshahi Division and lowest in Barishal Division. By 2022, however, Barishal had the highest proportion of people experiencing financial hardship while seeking treatment, while Dhaka Division had the lowest.

Rural residents are more likely than urban residents to face financial hardship when seeking medical care. People in rural areas also spend more out of their own pockets on treatment than those living in cities.

Researchers found that healthcare-related financial hardship is concentrated mainly among the poorest sections of society. The burden affects 90.8 per cent of people in the poorest group, compared with 13.6 per cent among the wealthiest.

Would increasing government allocations to the health sector solve the problem? Researchers said there was no guarantee that simply increasing public funding would ensure that poorer people benefited adequately.

The event opened with welcome remarks from S M Abu Horayra, director (research) of the Health Economics Unit. Mohammad Touhidul Islam, a national programme officer at the WHO, spoke about indicators under the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Sayem Ahmed, a national consultant for the WHO, presented the study’s methodology online from the United Kingdom.

Public health experts, health economists, university teachers, representatives of donor agencies and officials from private organisations attended the event.

The event was chaired by Mohammad Enamul Haque, director general of the Health Economics Unit. He said the study had brought to light some harsh truths that could not be denied. The research itself, he added, contained pathways towards solutions.

item.title: Police to recruit 4,000 SI directly; special BCS exam to recruit 400–500 ASP
item.description:
The government will directly recruit 4,000 sub-inspectors (SIs) into Bangladesh Police. The decision came at a meeting of the Secretaries’ Committee on Administrative Development at the Secretariat on Wednesday afternoon.

The government has amended the Police Regulations of Bengal (PRB) to facilitate direct recruitment to the SI posts.

Under the Police Regulations, 50 per cent of SI posts were previously filled through departmental promotions, while the remaining 50 per cent were filled through direct recruitment.

Under the existing rules, half of the 4,000 SI posts were also supposed to be filled through departmental promotions. However, the government will not follow that arrangement this time. For the first time, all 4,000 SIs will be recruited directly.

In addition, the government will recruit 10,000 new constables. The Secretaries’ Committee approved a proposal to recruit a total of 14,000 new personnel into the police force, including SIs and constables.

A senior Home Ministry official told Prothom Alo that the recruitment process for all 14,000 posts would be completed by December this year. However, the decision to recruit SIs directly by amending the regulations could cause resentment among police personnel awaiting promotion to the posts.

According to those concerned, direct recruitment of 4,000 SIs would deprive promotion-seekers of opportunities. If the government continues to recruit directly in the same way, the sense of deprivation could grow, potentially leading to frustration among police personnel performing duties at the field level.

Sources at the Cabinet Division and the Home Ministry said that the previous Awami League government recruited around 120,000 personnel to the posts of constable, SI and police sergeant during its 15-and-a-half years in power. This represented nearly half of the total strength of the police force.

According to officials, much of the recruitment over the past 15 years was politically motivated. The Awami League government of the time used police personnel on various occasions to remain in power.

Senior Home Ministry Secretary Manzur Morshed Chowdhury told Prothom Alo, “Direct recruitment to SI posts will take place to maintain normal law and order amid the changed circumstances. In addition, 10,000 new constables will be recruited. The Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Public Administration have approved the creation of these new posts. We have amended the Police Regulations to facilitate direct recruitment. However, this arrangement will apply only once. The government may also recruit directly in the future if it considers it necessary.”

Home Ministry sources said that after securing a landslide victory in the 13th parliamentary election and taking office, the BNP government found that very few personnel in the police administration shared its own ideological outlook.

Decisions taken to improve law and order were not being implemented properly. Although eight months had passed since the government took office, law and order had not improved as expected.

In addition, significant amounts of information were being leaked both within the country and abroad. The government decided to recruit SIs directly after considering these factors.

Home Ministry sources further said that the Police Headquarters initially sent a proposal to the Home Ministry to amend the Police Regulations. The Home Ministry then forwarded the proposal to the Ministry of Public Administration, which sent the proposal for 14,000 new personnel to the Ministry of Finance for approval.

After the Ministry of Finance approved it, the proposal was placed before the Secretaries’ Committee on Administrative Development on Wednesday.

The Secretaries’ Committee on Administrative Development is a high-level committee comprising the secretaries of 14 ministries. It makes important administrative decisions on behalf of the government.

The Cabinet Secretary chaired Wednesday’s meeting. The committee approves proposals to create new posts across various government departments.

Home Ministry sources said that the government would hold a special Bangladesh Civil Service (BCS) examination to recruit assistant superintendents of police (ASPs). This could be the 52nd BCS examination, through which the government would recruit between 400 and 500 ASPs. Authorities are considering shortening their basic training period to some extent after recruitment.

Home Ministry officials said that the authorities would exercise the utmost caution when recruiting the new police personnel. They would verify candidates against intelligence information before making final appointments.

item.title: Mahbubul Alam Hanif sentenced to death for crimes against humanity
item.description:
The International Crimes Tribunal-2 has sentenced Mahbubul Alam Hanif, joint general secretary of the Awami League (whose activities have been banned in the country), to death in a case filed on charges of crimes against humanity committed during the July mass uprising.

A three-member tribunal led by Justice Nozrul Islam Chowdhury delivered the verdict on Thursday. The other two members of the tribunal are Judges Md Manjurul Bashid and Nur Mohammad Shahriar Kabir.

The tribunal sentenced the three other accused in the case to imprisonment for the remainder of their lives. They are Sadar Uddin Khan, president of Kushtia district Awami League and former chairman of the district council; Asgar Ali, general secretary of Kushtia district Awami League and Ataur Rahman, general secretary of Kushtia municipality Awami League.

All four accused, including Hanif, are absconding. The tribunal-2 also ordered the confiscation of half of their property.

3 charges

The accused faced three charges in the case.

The first charge states that Mahbubul Alam Hanif was present alongside Awami League general secretary Obaidul Quader on 15, 17 and 30 July 2024 and endorsed Quader’s provocative statements.

It also alleges that at a discussion at the National Press Club on 29 July, Hanif labelled protesters as members of Jamaat, terrorists and communal forces, and instructed, incited, instigated and assisted others to kill and torture them.

According to the second charge, on Hanif’s instructions, Sadar Uddin Khan, Asgar Ali, Ataur Rahman and other Awami League leaders held a meeting at the Kushtia district Awami League office on 27 July 2024. At the meeting, the peaceful movement of unarmed students and citizens was described as terrorist activity. Awami League activists were instructed to use maximum force to suppress the movement in Kushtia city.

The third charge alleges that on 5 August 2024, following instructions from the four accused, goons from the Awami League and its affiliated organisations opened fire on students and members of the public at various locations in Kushtia city. Six people were killed in the shootings that day. They were Ashraful Islam, Suruj Ali, Abdullah Al Mustakin, Md Usama, Babul Farazi and Yusuf Sheikh.

According to information provided by the prosecution, the investigation into the case began on 25 March last year. The investigation agency submitted its report to the Office of the Chief Prosecutor on 11 September that year.

The prosecution subsequently submitted the formal charges to the tribunal on 6 October. After hearings from both sides, the tribunal ordered the formal framing of charges in the case on 2 November.

The trial formally began on 8 December last year with the presentation of opening statements. Witness testimony began the same day. The examination of witnesses concluded on 23 April this year, with a total of 19 witnesses testifying in the case.

The closing arguments in the case were completed on 10 June. On the same day, the tribunal kept the case awaiting the verdict. The prosecution later presented additional witnesses and documents.

Both the prosecution and the defence then presented arguments on the new testimony and documents. The arguments concluded on 7 October, after which the case was again kept awaiting the verdict.

Last Tuesday, Tribunal-2 ordered that the verdict in the case would be announced today, Thursday.

item.title: Bangladesh’s LDC graduation postponed by 3 years to November 2029
item.description:
Bangladesh’s graduation from the least developed country (LDC) category has been postponed by another three years. Instead of 24 November 2026, the country will now graduate in November 2029. This gives Bangladesh an additional three years to prepare.

The decision was approved at a plenary meeting of the United Nations General Assembly, which began at 1:00 am today, Friday. The meeting was chaired by UN General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman. UN Web TV broadcast the meeting live.

At the beginning of the meeting, Uruguay’s representative, speaking on behalf of the G-77, tabled a draft proposal to defer the LDC graduation of Bangladesh and Nepal by three years. No country’s representative opposed the proposal.

Representatives of France, Canada and Ireland, the latter speaking on behalf of the European Union, expressed support for postponing the graduation of Bangladesh and Nepal. However, all of them called for reforms in Bangladesh in their statements.

Bangladesh’s preparations for LDC graduation weak: UN report
Bangladesh was scheduled to graduate from the list of least developed countries on 24 November 2026. Following graduation, Bangladesh would become a fully-fledged developing country.

On 21 July, the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) recommended that the UN General Assembly take the final decision on Bangladesh’s request for an extension of its preparatory period for LDC greaduation.

Earlier, after reviewing Bangladesh’s application, the UN Committee for Development Policy (CDP) had recommended that the request by Bangladesh and Nepal to extend their preparatory periods be placed before the General Assembly for consideration. Based on that recommendation, ECOSOC decided to refer the matter to the General Assembly.

The final decision to extend the LDC preparatory period was taken today.

Bangladesh was scheduled to graduate from the list of least developed countries on 24 November 2026. Following graduation, Bangladesh would become a fully-fledged developing country.

The United Nations divides its member states into two categories: developed and developing countries. Countries on the LDC list are also developing countries. Those that lag behind other developing countries and require assistance from other nations are classified as least developed countries.

In 2021, the CDP made its final recommendation that Bangladesh graduate from the LDC category in 2024. However, the graduation was deferred by two years because of the Covid-19 pandemic.

Why the request for postponement

The policy of remaining firm on Bangladesh’s graduation from the least developed country (LDC) category in 2026 continued till the tenure of the interim government led by Professor Muhammad Yunus. However, after the BNP government took office in February this year, Bangladesh formally applied for a three-year postponement of its graduation from the LDC list.

The government argued that an extension would provide the necessary policy space to stabilise the macroeconomy, consolidate ongoing reforms, and complete priority activities under the Smooth Transition Strategy (STS).

Bangladesh’s letter also stated that the five-year preparatory period for LDC graduation had been ‘severely disrupted’ by a series of domestic and international crises.

Global crises included the lingering effects of the Covid-19 pandemic, a slow global economic recovery, the Russia-Ukraine war and the resulting volatility in energy and food markets, tighter global financial conditions, delays in the recovery of trade, instability in the Middle East and growing uncertainty in the global trading system.

Domestic challenges included irregularities in the financial sector, the political transition following the mass uprising of 2024, and the unresolved repatriation of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar.

LDC graduation: What needs to be done after applying for an extension

Bangladesh’s position

Bangladesh was included in the list of least developed countries (LDCs) in 1975. As an LDC, it has since enjoyed various benefits, including duty-free access for its exports. The United Nations Committee for Development Policy (CDP) makes recommendations on which countries should graduate from the LDC category.

LDCs are assessed every three years. A country’s eligibility for graduation is determined on the basis of three indicators: per capita income, human assets, and climate and economic vulnerability. A country must meet the thresholds for any two of the three indicators, or its per capita income must be twice the required threshold. These criteria, however, change over time.

Bangladesh met the thresholds for all three indicators in the 2018 and 2021 triennial reviews. These are gross national income (GNI), the Human Assets Index (HAI) and the Economic Vulnerability Index (EVI).

In 2021, the CDP made its final recommendation that Bangladesh graduate from the LDC category in 2024. However, the graduation was deferred by two years because of the Covid-19 pandemic; otherwise, Bangladesh would have graduated two years earlier. Now, a further three years have been added to the preparatory period for graduation.

item.title: A watershed moment: Bangladesh joins the global fight against rice methane
item.description:
This past week, I attended an event in Dhaka that will likely go down in history as a watershed moment for Bangladesh. Our country formally joined a global movement to rein in methane emissions, particularly from the agricultural sector.
With the next UN Climate Change Conference, COP31, scheduled for November 9-20, 2026, the timing could not be more opportune. This strategic move allows Bangladesh to arrive on the global stage with a powerful, demonstrable commitment to curbing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.
On Tuesday, Bangladesh formally joined AcceLER (Accelerating Scaling of Low-Emissions Rice in Southeast Asia). The initiative is designed to help countries plan, implement, and track effective methane mitigation measures.
Through a combination of suitability mapping, robust monitoring systems, remote sensing, and institutional capacity building, several major Asian rice-producing economies -- including Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, the Philippines, and Indonesia -- are already benefiting from the program. Now, Bangladesh joins their ranks, aiming to substantially reduce the climate impact of its paddy fields.
Rice occupies three-fourths of Bangladesh’s cultivated land. It remains fundamental to national food security, rural employment, and smallholder livelihoods.
The irrigated Boro rice ecosystem is the country's most productive agricultural system, supplying about 55% of domestic production between December and May. However, its heavy reliance on groundwater and prolonged flooding makes it a major source of methane emissions.
Methane emissions from rice cultivation in Bangladesh are estimated at 32.4 MtCO₂e (million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent), making rice one of the country's largest sources of methane.
To put this figure into perspective, 32.4 MtCO₂e is roughly equivalent to the annual greenhouse gas emissions of 7.7 million gasoline-powered passenger vehicles, the annual electricity consumption of 6.3 million homes, or the amount of carbon sequestered by 535 million tree seedlings grown for a decade.
Methane is an extremely potent super-pollutant -- 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide over a 20-year period -- which means curbing these emissions can help prevent catastrophic climate change.
It is responsible for about 30% of recent global warming. Furthermore, methane contributes to the formation of ground-level ozone, which harms human health and reduces crop yields. Cutting methane emissions is among the fastest and most effective ways to slow the rise in global temperatures.
The primary driver of these high emissions is the continuous presence of irrigation water in rice fields. Over the decades, well-intentioned initiatives, such as canal excavation and heavily subsidized irrigation water pumped through tube wells, have entrenched farming practices that rely on prolonged flooding. Continuously flooding croplands during the dry Boro season has come at a considerable environmental cost.
Today, this agricultural system faces growing challenges from declining groundwater levels, soaring irrigation costs, high energy consumption, and severe climate risks.
Fortunately, practical solutions exist. Water-saving practices, such as alternate wetting and drying (AWD), improved nutrient management through techniques like fertilizer deep placement, direct seeded rice (DSR), and short-duration rice varieties, can significantly reduce emissions by limiting the prolonged oxygen-deprived conditions that encourage methane-producing bacteria.
Instead of keeping fields permanently flooded, AWD requires farmers to allow water levels to fall periodically, exposing the soil to air. The resulting influx of oxygen suppresses methane production, significantly reducing emissions while conserving increasingly depleted groundwater resources.
Historically, methane emissions have been difficult to measure, making it challenging for governments to take effective action. Today, advanced satellite technologies offer greater transparency, helping authorities identify emission sources more accurately.
Since about 60% of methane emissions come from human activities, access to open, reliable data is essential for policymakers, scientists, and industry leaders to collaborate across borders.
Building on these technological advances, the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) recently brought together government agencies, researchers, and development partners in Dhaka to strengthen Bangladesh's capacity for the measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) of agricultural greenhouse gas emissions.
Dr Humnath Bhandari, who has headed IRRI's operations in Bangladesh for many years, highlighted digital MRV as a promising, affordable, and accurate way to track progress on a large scale. By mapping the extent to which farmers have adopted low-methane technologies, authorities can design more targeted and effective interventions.
Bangladesh can draw inspiration from its neighbours. On the sidelines of the Dhaka event, Dr Bjoern Ole Sander, an IRRI senior scientist and climate change mitigation team lead who heads the institute's operations in Thailand, shared how the organization has helped millions of Thai farmers transition to low-emission rice production across 100,000 hectares in six provinces.
While Thailand is a net rice exporter, Bangladesh remains structurally vulnerable. Despite being the world's third-largest rice producer, the country frequently relies on imports because of its high per capita rice consumption and a population that grows by around two million people annually. This vulnerability is compounded by crop losses caused by floods and other disasters.
Scaling up science-based, transparent low-emission practices is no longer optional; it is a priority for the country's long-term food security and climate resilience. By successfully implementing the AcceLER initiative, Bangladesh stands to reap significant benefits:
Transitioning to cleaner farming practices could also contribute to more liveable cities and healthier, more resilient communities across the country. The tools are available, the framework is in place, and the timing is right.
The challenge now is for Bangladesh's agricultural extension services to have the capacity and commitment to bring these practical, water-saving technologies out of the laboratories and into farmers' fields.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: HSC results hit six-year low as pass rate, GPA-5 numbers decline
item.description:
Bangladesh's Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations have recorded their lowest pass rate and number of GPA-5 achievers in six years, raising fresh concerns over learning outcomes, classroom teaching and the overall quality of secondary education.
The combined pass rate across the country's 11 education boards fell to 52.12% in 2026, down 6.71 percentage points from 58.83% last year. Meanwhile, the number of students achieving the highest grade, GPA-5, dropped to 40,084 from 69,097 in 2025.
The results, published yesterday, show that 646,685 students passed out of 1,270,583 candidates who appeared for examinations under the general, madrasa and technical education boards.
Education Minister ANM Ehsanul Haque Milon described this year's results as unsatisfactory, saying shortcomings in students' learning had become evident in their examination performance.
He said the government would identify weaknesses in the learning process and take necessary measures to address them.
A comparison of HSC and equivalent examination results from 2021 to 2026 shows a sustained downward trend in the overall pass rate, with particularly sharp declines over the past two years.
In 2021, the pass rate stood at 95.26%. It fell to 85.95% in 2022, 78.64% in 2023 and 77.78% in 2024.
The decline accelerated in 2025, when the pass rate dropped to 58.83%. This year, it fell further to 52.12%.
Overall, the pass rate has declined by 43.14 percentage points since 2021.
The number of students securing GPA-5 has also declined considerably over the past six years.
In 2021, a record 189,169 students achieved GPA-5. The figure declined in 2022 before falling to 92,595 in 2023.
It rose again to 145,911 in 2024 but dropped sharply to 69,097 in 2025.
This year, only 40,084 students secured the highest grade, 29,013 fewer than last year.
Compared with 2024, the number of GPA-5 achievers has fallen by 105,827.
The simultaneous decline in the pass rate and the number of GPA-5 achievers indicates a significant shift in examination outcomes. However, further analysis is needed to determine the extent to which changes in assessment standards, teaching quality and students' preparedness contributed to the decline.
This year's results show that female students outperformed their male counterparts in terms of the overall pass rate.
Of the students who passed, 356,528 were female and 290,157 were male, meaning 66,371 more girls passed than boys.
However, boys maintained a slight lead in the number of GPA-5 achievers, with 20,363 male students securing the highest grade, compared with 19,721 female students.
Institution-level results have also highlighted disparities in educational performance across the country.
While 139 institutions achieved a 100% pass rate, 293 recorded no successful candidates this year.
The number of institutions with a zero pass rate increased by 91 compared with last year.
The results have raised questions about classroom teaching, teacher availability, institutional management and students' academic preparedness, particularly at institutions where none of the candidates managed to pass.
Speaking at the results publication event, Education Minister ANM Ehsanul Haque Milon said the overall performance was unsatisfactory.
He acknowledged that the decline in the pass rate from last year was unacceptable and pointed to shortcomings in the learning process.
"The learning gaps among students have become evident in the results. We need to identify where the weaknesses lie and take necessary measures," he said.
The minister said the government had a responsibility to reassess existing teaching methods and determine the corrective steps needed.
He also expressed concern over possible errors in the published results, saying a review would help establish whether there had been any irregularities or inaccuracies.
Emphasising the need for greater transparency in future examinations, Milon said the prime minister wanted examination scripts to be properly evaluated to ensure that no student was unfairly assessed or deprived of their deserved results.
Prime Minister's Education Adviser Mahdi Amin presented various statistical aspects of the results at the publication event.

item.title: PM holds meeting over garment workers’ violent protests
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Sunday held a meeting with the home affairs and labour and employment ministers and other relevant officials amid a volatile situation triggered by violent readymade garment workers’ protests and clashes with police over their demand for a minimum monthly wage of Tk 30,000.

The meeting was held in the Cabinet Division conference room at the Secretariat in the evening.

Since the morning, protests, road blockades and vehicle arson had been reported in Mirpur in the capital, Kaliakair in Gazipur, and the industrial areas of Savar and Ashulia in Dhaka district. Around 300 factories in these areas declared holidays following the unrest.

Law enforcement agencies said leaders and activists of the Awami League (whose activities have been banned in the country) and its affiliated and associate organisations had joined the violent workers’ protests in Dhaka and Gazipur.

Among them was Sajmul Islam, organising secretary of the Jagannath University unit of Bangladesh Chhatra League, who led a procession in Kaliakair, Gazipur. Photographs of him leading the procession have circulated on social media.

Nine people affiliated with the Awami League, Sramik League and Chhatra League were arrested in Gazipur, while another 11 from the organisations were arrested in Mirpur.

Readymade garment workers in Gazipur began protesting and blockading roads at around 9:00 am, demanding that the minimum monthly wage be raised to Tk 30,000. Incidents of violence were also reported.

Traffic on the Dhaka–Tangail highway resumed at 3:00 pm after being suspended for nearly six hours because of the blockade.

In Mirpur, garment workers also staged protests and blocked roads over the same demand. Clashes and chases between protesters and police broke out repeatedly between 11:00 am and 1:00 pm.

At one point, protesters set fire to a police vehicle beneath Mirpur 11 metro station. Following the clashes, Mirpur 10, Mirpur 11 and Pallabi metro stations remained closed from noon until 2.30 pm.

Against this backdrop, the prime minister met ministers and advisers from the relevant ministries. 

Sources familiar with the meeting said those present included Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed, Labour and Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury, State Minister for Local Government Mir Shahe Alam, the prime minister’s adviser Mahdi Amin, and Shamsur Rahman Shimul Biswas, chief coordinator of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party’s labour organisation, Jatiyatabadi Sramik Dal.

Earlier in the afternoon, Labour Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury met the prime minister to discuss the ongoing labour unrest in the garment industry and the overall situation.

The minister cancelled his planned visit to the United Arab Emirates (UAE) because of the protests.

At a press conference at the Secretariat on Sunday morning, the labour minister announced the formation of a new wage board to determine the minimum wage for garment workers.

Ariful Haque Choudhury said the government had already informed the media and representatives of workers and employers that the wage board would be formed on Sunday following discussions with them.

Despite this, the workers’ road blockades were causing public hardship, he said, urging the protesters to return to their workplaces.

item.title: Govt forms six-member wage board for garment workers amid protests
item.description:
The government has formed a six-member wage board to review the minimum wage structure for garment workers amid protests across industrial areas, including Dhaka and Gazipur, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000.
Labour and Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury announced the formation of the board at a press briefing at his ministry on Sunday and urged the protesting workers to return to work instead of taking to the streets.
The ministry also issued separate gazette notifications on the formation of the minimum wage board for garment workers on Sunday.
The board has been constituted under Section 138 of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006 (amended in 2026), with the mandate to determine the minimum wage for workers in the garment industry under Section 139 of the law.
Senior District and Sessions Judge Sheikh Ashfakur Rahman has been appointed chairman of the board.
Prof Dr Mosleh Uddin Ahmed of the Department of Public Administration at Dhaka University has been appointed as its neutral member.
As general representatives, Asif Ayub, joint secretary general of the Bangladesh Employers Federation, has been appointed as the employers' representative, while Anwar Hossain, president of the Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Sramik Dal, will represent workers.
The board will also have two representatives from the garment industry: ABM Shamsuddin, a director of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), will represent employers, while Babul Akhtar, general secretary of the Bangladesh Garments and Industrial Workers Federation (BGIWF), will represent workers.
The formation of the wage board comes as garment workers have been staging demonstrations and blocking roads in different industrial areas, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000.
On Sunday, workers blocked the Mirpur-10 intersection in Dhaka and several points of the Dhaka-Tangail Highway in Gazipur, disrupting traffic.
Clashes between workers and police in Gazipur also prompted authorities to close most factories in the affected areas.

item.title: Bangladesh garment workers stage fourth day of wage protests
item.description:
Garment workers in Bangladesh staged a fourth day of wage protests on Tuesday, with police firing tear gas to disperse demonstrators as unrest disrupted factory operations and transport links in the country’s vital export sector.

The unrest, which began on Saturday, has intensified despite the government’s move to form a six-member wage board to review pay in Bangladesh’s garment sector, the world’s second-largest apparel exporter after China.

It comes at a critical time for manufacturers entering the peak production season for spring and summer export orders. The industry employs about 4 million workers, supplies global brands such as H&M, Zara and Gap, and accounts for more than 80 per cent of the country’s export earnings.

Clashes were reported across industrial belts around Dhaka, including Ashulia, Gazipur and the capital’s Mirpur area, as workers staged fresh demonstrations and attempted to block major highways. Dozens of people, including several police officers, were injured in the clashes.

H&M assessing any potential impact

In Ashulia, police fired tear gas and sound grenades after protesters threw bricks and stones at law enforcement personnel, said Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of Ashulia Industrial Police. Similar crowd-control measures were used in Dhaka’s Mirpur area, police said.

Additional security forces were deployed to contain the unrest, police said. Several factories in Gazipur and Ashulia again suspended operations or declared holidays after nearly 700 factories shut a day earlier.

“There are no major disruptions in our supply chain with only a limited number of factories temporarily closed,” H&M told Reuters. “We are assessing any potential impact on our overall production and supply chain.”

The Swedish company added it wanted adequate compensation for garment workers and remained committed to improving wages and working conditions.

Workers demand higher minimum wage

Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($245), up from the current 12,500 taka, arguing that rising living costs and persistent inflation have eroded their purchasing power. Several factories were also vandalised during the unrest.

“It is crucial that brands act immediately and speak out in support of workers’ demands,” said Anne Bienias, from the Clean Clothes Campaign industry advocacy group.

Industry officials warn prolonged closures could delay shipments and damage Bangladesh’s reputation as a reliable sourcing hub as it competes with rivals such as Vietnam and India for global apparel orders.

The wage dispute comes amid mounting pressure on workers from rising prices. The government formed the wage board on November 1 to review pay in the garment sector, but the move has yet to calm the protests.

Factory owners said they are contending with rising operating costs, uncertainty in energy markets linked to conflict in the Middle East, and softer demand in key export markets.

They warn that prolonged unrest could disrupt production schedules and jeopardise export orders, while workers continue to press for higher wages and better working conditions.

item.title: Why int’l airfares from Dhaka so high, parliamentary committee asks
item.description:
The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Public Undertakings has questioned why airfares from Dhaka to various international destinations are comparatively high.

It has advised the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) to examine whether a policy could be introduced to regulate fares.

At a meeting held at the Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban (parliament building) on Monday, the committee reviewed the financial management, operational activities and audit reports of Biman Bangladesh Airlines Limited and the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh.

According to sources concerned, the committee pointed out that the distance between Kuala Lumpur and Manila is roughly the same as that between Dhaka and Kuala Lumpur. Yet a ticket from Dhaka to Kuala Lumpur costs several times as much as one from Kuala Lumpur to Manila. The committee sought to know the reason for this disparity and whether any policy governed fare-setting.

In response, it was told that CAAB had no policy governing fares on international routes and that airlines set their own prices. The committee then suggested examining whether guidelines could be introduced for fare-setting.

According to the sources, the meeting also discussed Biman’s audit objections.

The committee asked whether a time-bound action plan, supported by evidence, could be submitted to address 18 objections.

It also sought to know whether action had been taken against those responsible for decisions to purchase defective aircraft, inoperative equipment, unnecessary spare-parts and the acquisition of old aircraft.

The committee further asked how irregularities involving Tk 7.36 billion had occurred in chartered cargo flights on the Dhaka–Guangzhou–Dhaka route and in revenue collection.

A press release issued by the Parliament Secretariat after the meeting said detailed information had been sought on the total amount recovered against the audit objections raised, the amount still outstanding and the number of people against whom disciplinary action had been taken.

The committee also stressed the need to submit time-bound action plans, backed by evidence, for each audit objection, the release added.

According to the media release, the committee recommended that Biman and the relevant authorities take the necessary steps to present detailed written explanations and supporting information on the issues raised at the next meeting.

The committee also sought explanations from the relevant authorities about why aircraft carrying the prime minister had repeatedly suffered technical problems.

Irregularities in Biman Bangladesh Airlines’ procurement of aircraft and equipment, as well as potential revenue losses arising from weaknesses in its IT systems, were also discussed.

According to the sources, Biman representatives said the most modern aircraft in its fleet were always assigned to the prime minister’s travel. The aircraft’s flight history over the preceding month was reviewed to check for any technical faults. A four-member investigation committee has been formed to determine the cause of the latest technical problem.

Some committee members also expressed dissatisfaction with the lift, services and overall environment of the VIP lounge at Dhaka’s international airport, the sources said.

One member remarked at the meeting that Biman tickets appeared to be unavailable when checked online, yet many seats were found to be empty after boarding.

According to the sources, Biman submitted a report on its operations at the meeting, outlining several reasons for flight delays.

The report said international check-in counters were insufficient, preventing them from closing on time and causing delays. Multiple flights were assigned to the same gate, while boarding bridges were also in short supply. Space was limited in the departure baggage area, and there were too few arrival baggage belts. The domestic terminal had only four check-in counters.

The meeting was chaired by committee chairman and Chief Whip of Parliament Nurul Islam Moni.

Committee members who attended included Whip Miah Nuruddin Ahmad Apu, Whip Md Akhtaruzzaman Mia, Khondoker Abu Ashfaque, Mohamed Koysor Ahmed, Biswas Jahangir Alam, Muhammad Nazibur Rahman and Mohammed Kamal Hossain.

item.title: Shama hopes India will make the right decision for Ganges water sharing treaty
item.description:
Bangladesh is hopeful of renewing the Ganges Water Sharing Treaty with India before its expiry this year, with the government preparing to negotiate on the basis of the country’s legitimate water requirements and long-term national interests.

“We believe and hope that the treaty, which expires this year, will be renewed. We hope India will make the right decision,” State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam told journalists at the foreign ministry on Monday afternoon.

The state minister said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman had already constituted a committee to conduct negotiations with India over the future of the water-sharing arrangement, which is due to expire in December.

She said the Water Resources Minister and the government’s Finance Adviser were leading the process, with representation from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Shama said discussions with India were already taking place at different working levels, while formal negotiations would be held to address outstanding issues.

“Formal discussions will be held with India. Discussions on the treaty are already taking place with them at various working levels,” she said.

The state minister expressed hope that the forthcoming negotiations would produce positive results and help ensure continued cooperation between the two neighbouring countries on sharing Ganges waters.

Asked whether Bangladesh was seeking a straightforward renewal of the existing treaty or a new agreement incorporating revised provisions, she indicated that the government’s negotiating position would be determined through the committee’s deliberations.

She stressed that Bangladesh would pursue its legitimate demands and prioritise the country’s present and future water requirements.

“Our negotiations will proceed on the basis of our rightful demands and what Bangladesh and its people need,” she said.

“We will take decisions in a way that best serves our future interests and helps resolve our water problems,” she added.

The state minister’s remarks come as the existing 30-year Ganges Water Sharing Treaty, signed between Bangladesh and India in 1996, approaches its expiry in December 2026.

Govt targets 3,000-4,000MW of solar power ahead of next summer
item.description:
The government aims to generate 3,000-4,000 megawatts of electricity from solar power ahead of next summer to help keep power shortages at a manageable level, State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Anindya Islam Amit said on Monday.
As part of the initiative, the government is promoting rooftop solar systems at public universities, considering them a relatively simple and effective way to expand renewable energy generation.
Speaking at a consultation meeting on installing solar power systems at 31 public universities, organized by the University Grants Commission (UGC) in Agargaon, Dhaka.
The state minister Amit said the government was working to prevent a repeat of the electricity-related hardship experienced by consumers during the current summer.
A solar power policy was formulated within two months to accelerate the expansion of solar energy, he said, adding that it could be revised based on feedback from relevant stakeholders.
The state minister emphasized that the initiative would not be imposed on universities. Decisions would instead be made based on each institution’s needs, capacity and practical circumstances, with support from the government and the UGC.
Amit said the expansion of rooftop solar power could help universities reduce carbon emissions and create opportunities to earn carbon credits.
The Power Division would support universities in obtaining carbon credits in recognition of their emissions reductions, he added.
One carbon credit generally represents the reduction or removal of one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent. Credits may be sold after completing the required verification and certification processes.
The state minister also announced that the Bangladesh Solar Expo would be held in Dhaka on November 3-4 to promote the use of solar energy.
A separate expert meeting involving university vice-chancellors is also planned to discuss solar installations at public universities. He urged all vice-chancellors to participate.
Presiding over the meeting, UGC Chairman Professor Dr Mamun Ahmed said the consultation was organized to address confusion surrounding rooftop solar installations and gather feedback from relevant stakeholders.
The commission has already conducted a survey and formed a team to assess the feasibility of installing solar systems at its own premises and at different public universities, he said.
The UGC would provide technical assistance to universities, but no decision would be imposed on them, he added.
Mamun stressed the importance of adopting the operating expenditure (OPEX) model, under which a service provider typically finances, installs and operates a solar power system while the institution pays under an agreed contractual arrangement.
A significant portion of universities’ operating budgets goes towards electricity and gas bills, he said, adding that wider use of solar power could substantially reduce these expenses.
Referring to an initiative at Jashore University of Science and Technology (JUST), the UGC chairman said a solar power system was being pursued through a tripartite agreement under the OPEX model.
Similar arrangements could be introduced at other universities, he added.
The UGC chairman urged universities to incorporate carbon credit opportunities into their solar power plans from the outset.
He said institutions should establish mechanisms to measure the amount of carbon emissions avoided through solar power generation, which would be essential to pursuing carbon credits.
The UGC would also provide vice-chancellors with necessary guidelines, draft agreements and relevant information on installing solar systems, Mamun said.
Universities could begin implementation within a month if they took the initiative immediately, he added.
At the meeting, Professor Dr M Shamsul Alam, dean of Daffodil International University, and Tahmilur Rahman, senior assistant secretary at the Power Division, presented separate papers on rooftop solar installations at university buildings and the expansion of solar power under the OPEX model.
Among those present were Power Division Secretary Mirana Mahrook, UGC member Professor Dr Masuma Habib, JUST Vice-Chancellor Professor Dr Iarul Kabir, Bangladesh University Council president and BUET Vice-Chancellor Professor Dr SM Abdur Razzak, Rajshahi University Vice-Chancellor Professor Dr Md Faridul Islam, Hajee Mohammad Danesh Science and Technology University Vice-Chancellor Professor Dr M Enamullah, and UGC Secretary Dr Md Fakhrul Islam.
Other UGC members, senior officials and vice-chancellors of the 31 public universities also attended the meeting.

item.title: Cabinet clears draft law to expedite solar power installations
item.description:
The Cabinet on Monday gave approval – both in principle and final – to the draft Special Solar Power Installation Act, 2026, aimed at expediting the expansion of solar power installations across the country.
The approval came at the cabinet meeting held at the Bangladesh Secretariat with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman in the chair.
The draft law was placed to turn the Special Solar Power Ordinance, 2026, already promulgated, into an act.
“The draft law was placed before the cabinet meeting for the approval. The cabinet cleared it subject to vetting by the Legislative and Parliamentary Affairs Division,” Cabinet Secretary Dr Nasimul Ghani said while briefing reporters after the meeting.
He said the Special Solar Power Ordinance, 2026, was promulgated under Article 93(1) of the Constitution to expedite the expansion of special solar power installation activities.
Explaining the rationale for the draft law, Nasimul Ghani said an ordinance promulgated under Article 93(1) of the Constitution must be placed before parliament at its first meeting following the promulgation, as stipulated in Article 93(2).
Following the cabinet's approval, the draft law will be placed before parliament as a bill.
Once passed by parliament and assented to by the president, it will turn into an act.
The Cabinet Secretary said the proposed law would undergo parliamentary debate, during which changes could be made if necessary.

item.title: Cabinet approves draft Public Procurement (2nd Amendment) Act, 2026
item.description:
The cabinet on Monday gave approval to the draft of the Public Procurement (Second Amendment) Act, 2026, aiming to ensure greater transparency, accountability, equal treatment and open competition in government procurement.
The approval – both in principle and final – came at the 26th cabinet meeting of the current government, chaired by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman at the Bangladesh Secretariat.
Cabinet Secretary Dr Nasimul Ghani briefed reporters after the meeting.
The Public Procurement Act, 2006, which serves as the principal legal framework for government procurement, has so far been amended six times.
The latest amendment was made through the Public Procurement (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026, promulgated on September 21, 2026.
The ordinance was issued to introduce updated provisions aimed at protecting local industries and creating greater competition in procurement activities.
The proposed amendment includes special provisions for new, micro and small, women and disadvantaged bidders to ensure their participation in government procurement.
It also seeks to modernize the procedures under the open tendering method and expand the application of the limited tendering method to ensure a more equitable distribution of resources.
The draft law also aims to clarify provisions relating to professional misconduct and introduce alternative procurement arrangements to meet urgent state requirements.
The draft of the Public Procurement (Second Amendment) Act, 2026, was published on the websites of the Bangladesh Public Procurement Authority (BPPA) and the Implementation Monitoring and Evaluation Division (IMED) for public opinion.
An ordinance promulgated under Article 93(1) of the Constitution must be placed before Parliament at its first meeting following the promulgation, as stipulated in Article 93(2).
The cabinet gave final approval to the draft law, subject to vetting by the Legislative and Parliamentary Affairs Division.

item.title: Iran says ready to reopen Hormuz in two days if US agrees to demands
item.description:
Iran on Monday said it was ready to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Washington agrees to conditions, as US President Donald Trump issued his latest war threat at a rally for midterm elections.
A senior Iranian official said the offer to open the vital energy corridor, which follows intense efforts by mediators to stop a return to war, showed “good faith.”
Tehran has blockaded Hormuz since the war started in February, sending energy prices soaring and posing an electoral challenge for Trump. The narrow gateway to the energy-rich Gulf normally carries one-fifth of global oil consumption.
“The possibility of implementing this plan in two days is another indication of Iran’s good-faith approach,” foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told reporters at a briefing.
“We have stated that, if Iran’s demands are met, it would be possible to restore security to the Strait of Hormuz and resume the negotiating process within a short period.”
In September, Iran proposed a seven-day plan to reopen Hormuz if the US agreed to demands including ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending its counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Baqaei said messages were being exchanged with the United States via mediators, adding that “everything depends” on the US side accepting the Iranian demands.
“Only then can we discuss the subsequent stages.”
During final rallies for the US midterms on Tuesday, where diesel prices and consumer inflation are a key issue, Trump struck a belligerent tone, warning Iran to expect “the hammer.”
“The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can... But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer,” he told voters in Iowa.
Officials from Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye have held talks with Iran in recent days, while US Vice President JD Vance sent a letter to Tehran.
Oman’s ruler Sultan Haitham bin Tariq discussed the war with Chinese President Xi Jinping during a visit to Beijing on Monday, an Omani foreign ministry statement said.
“The two sides called for resolving disputes through political and diplomatic means, urging the United States and Iran to pursue a peaceful path, achieve a ceasefire (and) prevent war entirely,” it said, calling for “dialogue and negotiations as soon as possible,”
China’s top diplomat also told a senior Iranian official that Beijing supports Tehran in “safeguarding its own sovereignty and security,”
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi made the remarks to Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, according to a statement from Beijing.
“All parties should... in a spirit of reason and pragmatism, focus on a political solution rather than once again resorting to armed conflict,” Wang was cited as saying.
Bagheri told Wang that “Tehran’s stance on defending its national security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity remains unchanged, and that Iran will make no compromises in this regard,” according to state TV.
In an interview with Al Jazeera released on Sunday, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Washington must accept a new route agreed between Iran and Oman for transiting the strait.
He said the US must also remove sanctions imposed in recent months and reduce American troop numbers in the region.
Washington has since August rolled out a fresh raft of sanctions, part of what it called “economic asphyxiation” of Iran.
Trump’s “hammer” comment is just the latest threat to Tehran from the US and Israel, whose joint attack marked the start of the war on February 28.
On Saturday, Trump said he still had to “take care” of one or two targets including Pickaxe mountain in central Iran, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility.
“Any act of aggression against Iran, any military attack against Iran, by whatever means, will be met with a powerful, immediate and comprehensive response from us,” Baqaei said.
At the midterms, Democrats expect to win at least partial control of Congress and impose political constraints on Trump for the first time in two years.
